source: Climate Resilient Broadcasting Rice Growing Technique (ASPIRE/IFAD, MAFF, 2018); RULIP Project leaf-folder pest leaflet; CARDI Rice Pest brochure (FAO-funded, Plant Protection Program)
text:
Rice leaf folder (ដង្កូវមូរស្លឹក): moths lay eggs on leaves; larvae roll a leaf around themselves and scrape the green tissue from inside, leaving white streaky damage. Eggs hatch in about 4-6 days, larvae feed for roughly 15-30 days, and pupae take about 6-10 days, so a full generation completes in a few weeks. Damage is worse in dense, high-nitrogen canopies. Manage by avoiding excess nitrogen, keeping natural predators (spiders, dragonflies, parasitic wasps) intact, and only spraying if a real economic threshold of damaged leaves is reached during tillering -- not as a routine precaution.

Brown planthopper (ចំពាមផ្កាឬសអ្នកចំណីស្រូវ): feeds at the stem base, can cause 'hopper burn' (whole patches of rice drying out) and spreads viral disease between plants. It builds up fastest under heavy nitrogen use and continuous flooding without drainage, and is knocked back hardest by broad-spectrum insecticide use that also kills its natural enemies -- so the most reliable long-term control is a resistant variety plus conservative nitrogen use plus alternating wet-dry irrigation, saving insecticide for genuine outbreaks.

Other recurring rice pests include the rice bug (feeds on developing grain during the milk stage, reducing filled-grain percentage), gall midge (larvae damage the growing point, producing a hollow 'onion leaf' symptom instead of a normal panicle), grasshoppers (chew leaf tissue), and the golden apple snail (an invasive species first recorded in Cambodia in 1995 that can strip young seedlings within days of transplanting or early broadcast emergence -- controlled by hand-picking, keeping ducks in the field to graze snails, or physical barriers around vulnerable seedbeds).

Across all these pests, the general principle is the same: rely on field sanitation, resistant varieties, and conserving natural predators first; only reach for a pesticide once damage clearly exceeds an economic threshold, and always match the product and rate to the specific pest and current Cambodian registration rather than spraying broadly as a precaution.
